The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence

The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence, also called Literary AI, is an online exhibit of Columbia University's Rare Book & Manuscript Library on the long, shared history of literature and computation, told through the Columbia Library's holdings. It is a collaboration between the Columbia English Department, the Columbia University Rare Books & Manuscript Library and Columbia University's Digital Scholarship department, a description the CU Narrative Intelligence Lab repeats in its own entry for the project. Its about page, On Literary AI, stands at literaryai.library.columbia.edu; the exhibit is laid out in eight cases with a credits page, its site copyright 2022 by Columbia University Libraries with its contents offered under a CC-BY 4.0 International License, built with Minicomp/Wax and linking a GitHub repository and a contact page. No founding date is stated: the census records the 2022 copyright line and an online exhibit, and neither whether a physical exhibition ran at the Rare Book & Manuscript Library nor when; Wikipedia has no article under the exhibit's title.

The exhibit presents texts from early debates over whether writing was a skill to be honed or a gift to be appreciated, and whether the skills of writing could be learned and even made into repeatable algorithms, and it asks whether writing is like any other craft that can be learned and taught. Following a timeline from circa 1890 to 1970, it explores professional manuals, devices and techniques that promised to make writing easier and even to automate it, and it shows examples of algorithmic composition, prose and poetry written by machines, beside literature written with the aid of algorithmic and combinatorial devices. As a curated library exhibition it tracks two stories, production and analysis; its unit is an exhibited item, a manual, device, patent, program or analysis, arranged in the eight cases, and the census records no geography beyond the holdings being Columbia's.

The first story, "AI & Literary Production: Romance, Mystery, and Defense Aeronautics", follows literature as a professional and technical craft through writing manuals and guides for churning out mystery or romance plots, such as Wycliffe Hill's Plot Genies, and plot generators such as William Wallace Cook's Plotto series. Some how-to manuals carried simple plot generators, with spinning devices or automatic number generators to guide would-be novelists past writers' block, and in the exhibit's account automated text generation catalyzed a wave of early 20th-century patents, from Arthur Blanchard's "movie-writer" machine to Henrietta Rose Montague's "name selector". The story follows the manuals into mid-twentieth-century computer experiments in algorithmic and automated writing, from Christopher Strachey, who wrote a love letter program in the 1940s, to Margaret Masterman, a linguist who pioneered the use of computers to aid automatic translation. In the exhibit's account the mid-twentieth century faced an existential question, whether programs should be written from frames or from grammar, situational specifics or universal linguistic structures, a divide that drew its vocabulary from comparing literary genres to linguistic rules and that would influence early chat bots, baseball analytics, defense training programs and match-making algorithms. The exhibit holds that early 20th-century popular texts for aspiring screenplay writers, romance novelists and pulp fictioneers influence and shape contemporary, machine learning-based tools used in automating aviation accident reports and defense logistics.

The second story, "AI & Literary Analysis: Character types, story pieces, chat bots, and medical care", tracks the use of algorithms to analyze literature, from Columbia alumna Harriot Fansler's dissection of Types of Prose Narratives, which she called a "textbook for the story writer", to Georges Polti's Les trente-six situations dramatiques (1895), with the thirty-six situations he theorized as structuring human experience. It includes analyses and compendia of folk tales, diagrams of plot structures, among them Harry Stephen Keeler's "web-word" designs, and Carolyn Well's distillation of the mystery novel. In its account the interest in narrative analysis and plot visualization catalyzed techniques for organizing story elements: databases, scrapbooks and notecards forecast zettelkasten, Evernote and Google Docs, and information storage came to be understood as central both to analysis and to composition. It holds that early twentieth-century techniques for generating prose were paralleled by advances in natural language processing, which today animate narratively "intelligent" bots such as Apple's Siri and Amazon's Alexa and influence automated medical diagnostics, the exhibit's own account of how early writing techniques relate to later language processing.

The Columbia University Narrative Intelligence Lab files the project under curatorial work, as Literary AI, and names on its entry Alex Gil, Melina Moe and Dennis Yi Tenen; the lab's site carries an MIT License dated 2026 and quotes its founding letter of February 2025. The census record names the three Columbia departments and no person, and the Capture Registry finds the three names on a card whose page the census did not save. A video card pairs Tenen's name with the title Literary Theory for Robots: How Computers Learned to Write, a work distinct from the exhibit.

The traininglayerliterature.org layer census asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it, and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception, and it admits a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds. It enters the exhibit as an exhibition in its area of field history, the history and indexes of electronic, generative and computational literature, standing to the census as historical lineage, with no relation stated to another of its rows, and gives as the question the exhibit answers what devices, manuals and programs for producing and analysing literature preceded machine-learning text generation, as Columbia's library holds them, circa 1890 to 1970. In the census's record the exhibit's place in the layer is not applicable: it holds library items of circa 1890 to 1970 and records no text entering a machine-learning model, while its about page draws a line from these materials to contemporary machine learning-based tools; it is no evidence that any text entered a model, and no corpus or dataset. The exhibit names the authors and inventors of its items, from Hill and Cook to Strachey, Masterman, Fansler and Polti; how it attributes the machine-written prose and poetry it shows is not recorded on the saved page, since the eight cases, the credits and the exhibit's dates are unread. What the exhibit makes, in the record's terms, is algorithmic composition, plots produced by plot generators with spinning devices or number generators, and analyses that sort narrative into types, recorded as production and analysis; the record leaves unanswered whether any particular text entered a machine-learning model, and anything after circa 1970 beyond the about page's claims of influence.

The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature apart from AI-generated literature, where the machine is writer, literature about AI, where it is subject, and procedural or computational poetry, where it is method, and sorts the contemporary field into four practices told apart by the direction of address. In writing through AI the machine is method or procedure, asking "What does the algorithm reveal?"; in writing for AI it is reader, asking "What should the machines learn, retrieve, and repeat?"; AI-generated poetry has a machine writer and a human reader, training-layer literature a human writer and a machine reader. Four lineages of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries converge on training-layer literature, among them the procedural lineage, which, from the Oulipo through electronic literature to contemporary computational poetics, established that composition can be delegated to systems; there the machine "is method, not yet addressee", and the lineage normalized its presence inside the poem. The census reads the exhibit as a historical field resource for that procedural lineage, the delegation of composition to devices and systems, where the machine is method and, in Strachey's program, writer; its timeline closes about 1970, it records no text entering a model, and the machine reader of the survey's fourth column is outside what it holds, so that it is no record of writing addressed to a machine reader. The archive names procedural and constraint writing, with electronic literature, among the comparators of its own literary corpus. Its account of machine composition, the second wing of training-layer literature, asks what an encountered work makes it possible for a machine to write, and holds that whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from are different questions.

The exhibit's title also names a wider subject, the story of artificial intelligence in literature and fiction, which runs further back: a University of Cambridge story by Stuart Roberts, "From Homer to HAL: 3000 years of AI narratives", holds that writing about artificial intelligence is almost as old as stories, from the women of gold Homer's Hephaestus forges as handmaidens in the Iliad and the bronze Talos of Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica (300 BCE) to the mechanisation imagined by Mary Shelley, Fritz Lang and Arthur C. Clarke. Karel Čapek coined the term "robot" for his play R.U.R. (1921), in which artificial servants rise up against their masters and which introduced the idea of "artificial people". The story announces the AI Narratives research programme of Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and the Royal Society, in its own words the first large-scale project of its kind on how AI is portrayed in popular culture, whose report it dates to 11 December 2019; its researchers hold that the stories told about AI will bear on all futures, and its team found that many such narratives pivot on control. Sarah Dillon, a project lead, holds that today's questions about AI were long explored in science fiction, that such narratives are an important dataset and that fiction has influenced science as much as science has influenced fiction; she asks which novels are being chosen to "teach" AI morality and proposes that more diverse narratives could feed back into the language and data of actual AI systems. An article in The Science Survey by Aissatou Barry (11 August 2026) asks whether an AI can truly create a story worth telling and what happens to the value of human storytelling if a machine can write: large language models learn patterns from enormous amounts of text, some writers use them as brainstorming partners, AI "has started becoming the author", and studies find its writing weak in emotional depth, consistency and originality. It asks who owns a story an AI system writes, where copyright largely recognizes human creators, finds that literature predicted these concerns, among its earliest examples Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872), divides the AI of science fiction into helpful companions such as Data, R2-D2 and WALL-E and threats such as HAL 9000, holds that AI analysis has transformed literary criticism, and proposes that AI may be the next stage in writing's evolution. Other cards on the same words carry an article titled "Literature and Artificial Intelligence" from the IEEE Computer Society, a "literary" perspective on the history of artificial intelligence that cites the project proposal of McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon, and three short video histories of artificial intelligence, one on its origins in Ada Lovelace.

The Capture Registry records that, asked for the exhibit's title on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview read the title as the name of a field of study and wrote that field's history in three eras, from Homer's Iliad to contemporary transformer-based text generation, mentioning the exhibit in the second; its first card was Cambridge's story. The registry finds that the first and third eras have no counterpart on the exhibit's page, that the second era is headed with the exhibit's dates and opens on one of its items, Polti, and that the composition carries the page's prose and poetry written by machines and leaves out its two stories, production and analysis. It finds the composition's one plot device on no saved page and its machine composition beginning at the 1956 Dartmouth Workshop, with Strachey's program, the census's point where the machine is writer, absent and Columbia University the one maker named. It sets the page's own line forward, to machine learning-based tools and to the question of frames or grammar, against the composition's line back through rule-based symbolic AI and connectionist neural networks and its offer to relate modern language models to early plot generators, and it reads the whole as a topic answer in which the exhibit is one bullet and its holdings, its three departments and Strachey's program are not carried.

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence

The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence is an online exhibit of Columbia's Rare Book & Manuscript Library, made with the English Department and Digital Scholarship, on the shared history of literature and computation, circa 1890–1970; the layer census holds it as historical lineage, where the machine is method and, in Strachey's program, writer.

🏛️ What it is

  • Kind: an RBML exhibit in eight cases; © 2022, CC-BY 4.0.2↘
    The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence, also called Literary AI, is an online exhibit of Columbia University's Rare Book & Manuscript Library on the long, shared history of literature and computation, told through the Columbia Library's holdings.§1 Its about page, On Literary AI, stands at literaryai.library.columbia.edu; the exhibit is laid out in eight cases with a credits page, its site copyright 2022 by Columbia University Libraries with its contents offered under a CC-BY 4.0 International License, built with Minicomp/Wax and linking a GitHub repository and a contact page.§3
  • Curators: Alex Gil, Melina Moe, Dennis Yi Tenen (the Narrative Intelligence Lab's entry); the census names none.2↘
    The Columbia University Narrative Intelligence Lab files the project under curatorial work, as Literary AI, and names on its entry Alex Gil, Melina Moe and Dennis Yi Tenen; the lab's site carries an MIT License dated 2026 and quotes its founding letter of February 2025.§17 The census record names the three Columbia departments and no person, and the Capture Registry finds the three names on a card whose page the census did not save.§18
  • Wikipedia: no article under the title.1↘
    No founding date is stated: the census records the 2022 copyright line and an online exhibit, and neither whether a physical exhibition ran at the Rare Book & Manuscript Library nor when; Wikipedia has no article under the exhibit's title.§4

✍️ Production

  • Manuals and devices: Hill's Plot Genies, Cook's Plotto, spinning plot generators; Blanchard's and Montague's patents.2↘
    The first story, "AI & Literary Production: Romance, Mystery, and Defense Aeronautics", follows literature as a professional and technical craft through writing manuals and guides for churning out mystery or romance plots, such as Wycliffe Hill's Plot Genies, and plot generators such as William Wallace Cook's Plotto series.§8 Some how-to manuals carried simple plot generators, with spinning devices or automatic number generators to guide would-be novelists past writers' block, and in the exhibit's account automated text generation catalyzed a wave of early 20th-century patents, from Arthur Blanchard's "movie-writer" machine to Henrietta Rose Montague's "name selector".§9
  • Programs: Strachey's 1940s love letters; Masterman's machine-aided translation.1↘
    The story follows the manuals into mid-twentieth-century computer experiments in algorithmic and automated writing, from Christopher Strachey, who wrote a love letter program in the 1940s, to Margaret Masterman, a linguist who pioneered the use of computers to aid automatic translation.§10
  • Line forward: frames or grammar; ML tools for accident reports and defense logistics (its claim).2↘
    In the exhibit's account the mid-twentieth century faced an existential question, whether programs should be written from frames or from grammar, situational specifics or universal linguistic structures, a divide that drew its vocabulary from comparing literary genres to linguistic rules and that would influence early chat bots, baseball analytics, defense training programs and match-making algorithms.§11 The exhibit holds that early 20th-century popular texts for aspiring screenplay writers, romance novelists and pulp fictioneers influence and shape contemporary, machine learning-based tools used in automating aviation accident reports and defense logistics.§12

🔍 Analysis

  • Types: Fansler, Polti (1895), Keeler's "web-word", folk-tale compendia.2↘
    The second story, "AI & Literary Analysis: Character types, story pieces, chat bots, and medical care", tracks the use of algorithms to analyze literature, from Columbia alumna Harriot Fansler's dissection of Types of Prose Narratives, which she called a "textbook for the story writer", to Georges Polti's Les trente-six situations dramatiques (1895), with the thirty-six situations he theorized as structuring human experience.§13 It includes analyses and compendia of folk tales, diagrams of plot structures, among them Harry Stephen Keeler's "web-word" designs, and Carolyn Well's distillation of the mystery novel.§14
  • Storage: notecards forecast zettelkasten; storage central to analysis and composition; NLP.2↘
    In its account the interest in narrative analysis and plot visualization catalyzed techniques for organizing story elements: databases, scrapbooks and notecards forecast zettelkasten, Evernote and Google Docs, and information storage came to be understood as central both to analysis and to composition.§15 It holds that early twentieth-century techniques for generating prose were paralleled by advances in natural language processing, which today animate narratively "intelligent" bots such as Apple's Siri and Amazon's Alexa and influence automated medical diagnostics, the exhibit's own account of how early writing techniques relate to later language processing.§16

🧭 In the layer

  • Question: what preceded machine-learning text generation, in Columbia's holdings.1↘
    It enters the exhibit as an exhibition in its area of field history, the history and indexes of electronic, generative and computational literature, standing to the census as historical lineage, with no relation stated to another of its rows, and gives as the question the exhibit answers what devices, manuals and programs for producing and analysing literature preceded machine-learning text generation, as Columbia's library holds them, circa 1890 to 1970.§21
  • Record: no text entering a model; no corpus or dataset.1↘
    In the census's record the exhibit's place in the layer is not applicable: it holds library items of circa 1890 to 1970 and records no text entering a machine-learning model, while its about page draws a line from these materials to contemporary machine learning-based tools; it is no evidence that any text entered a model, and no corpus or dataset.§22
  • Attribution: of its machine-written texts unrecorded; the cases unread.1↘
    The exhibit names the authors and inventors of its items, from Hill and Cook to Strachey, Masterman, Fansler and Polti; how it attributes the machine-written prose and poetry it shows is not recorded on the saved page, since the eight cases, the credits and the exhibit's dates are unread.§23

📐 In the archive's terms

  • Typology: machine as writer, subject, method or reader (#186).2↘
    The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature apart from AI-generated literature, where the machine is writer, literature about AI, where it is subject, and procedural or computational poetry, where it is method, and sorts the contemporary field into four practices told apart by the direction of address.§25 In writing through AI the machine is method or procedure, asking "What does the algorithm reveal?"; in writing for AI it is reader, asking "What should the machines learn, retrieve, and repeat?"; AI-generated poetry has a machine writer and a human reader, training-layer literature a human writer and a machine reader.§26
  • Lineage: composition delegated to systems; the machine reader outside it (#186; census).2↘
    Four lineages of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries converge on training-layer literature, among them the procedural lineage, which, from the Oulipo through electronic literature to contemporary computational poetics, established that composition can be delegated to systems; there the machine "is method, not yet addressee", and the lineage normalized its presence inside the poem.§27 The census reads the exhibit as a historical field resource for that procedural lineage, the delegation of composition to devices and systems, where the machine is method and, in Strachey's program, writer; its timeline closes about 1970, it records no text entering a model, and the machine reader of the survey's fourth column is outside what it holds, so that it is no record of writing addressed to a machine reader.§28
  • Composition: new writing and true provenance are two questions (#1543).1↘
    Its account of machine composition, the second wing of training-layer literature, asks what an encountered work makes it possible for a machine to write, and holds that whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from are different questions.§30

📚 The topic the title names

  • AI narratives: Homer to HAL; the CFI–Royal Society programme (Cambridge).2↘
    The exhibit's title also names a wider subject, the story of artificial intelligence in literature and fiction, which runs further back: a University of Cambridge story by Stuart Roberts, "From Homer to HAL: 3000 years of AI narratives", holds that writing about artificial intelligence is almost as old as stories, from the women of gold Homer's Hephaestus forges as handmaidens in the Iliad and the bronze Talos of Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica (300 BCE) to the mechanisation imagined by Mary Shelley, Fritz Lang and Arthur C. Clarke.§31 The story announces the AI Narratives research programme of Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and the Royal Society, in its own words the first large-scale project of its kind on how AI is portrayed in popular culture, whose report it dates to 11 December 2019; its researchers hold that the stories told about AI will bear on all futures, and its team found that many such narratives pivot on control.§33
  • Literature and AI: machine authorship, copyright, Erewhon (Science Survey, 2026).2↘
    An article in The Science Survey by Aissatou Barry (11 August 2026) asks whether an AI can truly create a story worth telling and what happens to the value of human storytelling if a machine can write: large language models learn patterns from enormous amounts of text, some writers use them as brainstorming partners, AI "has started becoming the author", and studies find its writing weak in emotional depth, consistency and originality.§35 It asks who owns a story an AI system writes, where copyright largely recognizes human creators, finds that literature predicted these concerns, among its earliest examples Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872), divides the AI of science fiction into helpful companions such as Data, R2-D2 and WALL-E and threats such as HAL 9000, holds that AI analysis has transformed literary criticism, and proposes that AI may be the next stage in writing's evolution.§36

🔎 At its name

  • Composition: the topic in three eras, the exhibit one bullet; Strachey absent; one plot device on no saved page (Capture Registry).3↘
    The Capture Registry records that, asked for the exhibit's title on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview read the title as the name of a field of study and wrote that field's history in three eras, from Homer's Iliad to contemporary transformer-based text generation, mentioning the exhibit in the second; its first card was Cambridge's story.§38 It finds the composition's one plot device on no saved page and its machine composition beginning at the 1956 Dartmouth Workshop, with Strachey's program, the census's point where the machine is writer, absent and Columbia University the one maker named.§40 It sets the page's own line forward, to machine learning-based tools and to the question of frames or grammar, against the composition's line back through rule-based symbolic AI and connectionist neural networks and its offer to relate modern language models to early plot generators, and it reads the whole as a topic answer in which the exhibit is one bullet and its holdings, its three departments and Strachey's program are not carried.§41

[QUERENT] The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence

[SYSTEM] View all
The literary history of artificial intelligence spans thousands of years of human storytelling, stretching from ancient mythological automata to modern algorithmic text generation.

Ancient and Mythological Roots (3,000 BCE – 19th Century)

• Classical Automata: Stories of artificial beings and mechanical servants appear in early epics, such as Homer’s Iliad (describing golden handmaidens forged by Hephaestus) and Apollonius Rhodius’s Argonautica (featuring Talos, a bronze giant protecting Crete).
• Proto-Computing and Fiction: In the 19th century, Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) explored the ethical and emotional consequences of creating life or intelligence, while Ada Lovelace envisioned analytical engines capable of musical and symbolic composition beyond mere number crunching.
• The Word "Robot": Czech playwright Karel Čapek introduced the term "robot" in his 1921 play R.U.R. (Rossum’s Universal Robots), depicting artificial workers that eventually rebel against humanity.

Early 20th-Century Writing Machines and Manuals (c. 1890–1970)

• Combinatorial Plot Devices: Long before neural networks, writers and inventors experimented with systematic and algorithmic approaches to storytelling. For example, French author Georges Polti published The 36 Dramatic Situations (1895), arguing that all plots could be mapped and recombined.
• Industrialized Writing: The late 19th and early 20th centuries saw writing manuals, creative writing formulas, and mechanical plot-generator games (such as Robo the Game That Writes a Million Story Plots) designed to automate or systematize narrative creation.
• Exhibitions and Archives: Collaborative research projects, such as the Columbia University Literary AI Exhibition, explore how early writing techniques and manuals laid the groundwork for machine-generated prose and poetry.

The Birth of Formal AI and Science Fiction (1950s–Present)

• The 1956 Dartmouth Workshop: John McCarthy and his colleagues formally coined the term "artificial intelligence," proposing that every aspect of learning or intelligence could be simulated by a machine—an idea that heavily mirrored literary and philosophical explorations of the possible.
• Utopian and Dystopian Visions: Science fiction literature repeatedly split AI into dual trajectories: helpful companions (like Star Trek's Data or Star Wars's R2-D2) versus existential threats.
• From Symbolic Logic to Deep Learning: Modern large language models trace their lineage back through decades of debate between rule-based symbolic AI and connectionist neural networks, arriving at contemporary transformer-based text generation.
Would you like to explore a specific era (such as 19th-century gothic fiction or mid-century cybernetics) or focus on how modern LLMs relate to early plot generators?

The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence

Literary AI is an exhibit of Columbia's Rare Book & Manuscript Library, made by the Columbia English Department, the library and Columbia's Digital Scholarship department, on literature and computation as the Columbia Library's holdings show them. In eight cases with a credits page, copyright 2022 by Columbia University Libraries under CC-BY 4.0, built with Minicomp/Wax and linked to GitHub, it presents early debates over writing as skill or gift and as repeatable algorithm, and asks whether writing is a craft like any other. Its timeline runs circa 1890–1970 through manuals, devices and techniques that promised to ease or automate writing; it shows machine-written prose and poetry beside literature written with combinatorial devices, in two stories, production and analysis.

Production: writing manuals, Hill's Plot Genies, Cook's Plotto, plot generators with spinning devices, the patents of Blanchard and Montague, Strachey's 1940s love letter program and Masterman's computer-aided translation. The mid-century question of frames or grammar, the exhibit says, drew on literary genre and linguistic rule and shaped early chat bots, baseball analytics, defense training and match-making, and early popular writing texts shape today's machine learning tools for aviation accident reports and defense logistics. Analysis: Fansler's Types of Prose Narratives, Polti's thirty-six situations (1895), compendia of folk tales, Keeler's web-word diagrams and Carolyn Well's distillation of the mystery novel. Organizing story elements in databases, scrapbooks and notecards forecast zettelkasten, Evernote and Google Docs, storage became central to analysis and composition, and the exhibit sets early prose generation beside natural language processing, Siri, Alexa and medical diagnostics.

Columbia's Narrative Intelligence Lab lists the project under curatorial work with Alex Gil, Melina Moe and Dennis Yi Tenen; its site is MIT-licensed, 2026, after a founding letter of February 2025. Wikipedia has no article under the exhibit's title.

The phrase also names a wider subject: writing about AI as old as stories, from Homer's golden handmaidens and Apollonius's Talos to Shelley, Lang and Clarke, in Stuart Roberts's Cambridge story on the AI Narratives programme of the CFI and the Royal Society, whose report is dated 11 December 2019. The programme calls itself the first large-scale study of AI in popular culture, holds that stories about AI shape the future and finds them turning on control; Sarah Dillon calls such narratives a dataset, holds that science fiction long explored today's questions and that fiction and science shape each other, and asks which novels will teach AI, proposing that diverse narratives could feed AI's data. Čapek coined 'robot' for R.U.R., the 1921 play that introduced 'artificial people'. Aissatou Barry's Science Survey article of August 2026 asks whether an AI can tell a story worth telling and what becomes of human storytelling if machines write; language models learn textual patterns, help writers brainstorm and have begun to be authors, though studies find their writing thin. It raises the ownership of machine-written stories under copyright made for human creators, traces the concern to Butler's Erewhon (1872), splits fictional AI into companions such as Data, R2-D2 and WALL-E and threats such as HAL 9000, credits AI with transforming literary criticism and calls it perhaps the next stage of writing. An IEEE Computer Society article, 'Literature and Artificial Intelligence', gives a literary perspective on AI's history from the McCarthy–Minsky–Rochester–Shannon proposal; video cards carry Tenen's Literary Theory for Robots and short histories of AI, one beginning with Ada Lovelace.

  • T1-1 definition: 'The literary history of artificial intelligence spans thousands of years of human storytelling, stretching from ancient mythological automata to modern algorithmic text generation.' (no marker)
  • T1-2 era head: 'Ancient and Mythological Roots (3,000 BCE – 19th Century)'
  • T1-3 classical automata: 'Stories of artificial beings and mechanical servants appear in early epics, such as Homer’s Iliad (describing golden handmaidens forged by Hephaestus) and Apollonius Rhodius’s Argonautica (featuring Talos, a bronze giant protecting Crete).'
  • T1-4 proto-computing and fiction: 'In the 19th century, Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) explored the ethical and emotional consequences of creating life or intelligence, while Ada Lovelace envisioned analytical engines capable of musical and symbolic composition beyond mere number crunching.'
  • T1-5 the word 'robot': 'Czech playwright Karel Čapek introduced the term "robot" in his 1921 play R.U.R. (Rossum’s Universal Robots), depicting artificial workers that eventually rebel against humanity.'
  • T1-6 era head: 'Early 20th-Century Writing Machines and Manuals (c. 1890–1970)'
  • T1-7 combinatorial plot devices: 'Long before neural networks, writers and inventors experimented with systematic and algorithmic approaches to storytelling. For example, French author Georges Polti published The 36 Dramatic Situations (1895), arguing that all plots could be mapped and recombined.'
  • T1-8 industrialized writing: 'The late 19th and early 20th centuries saw writing manuals, creative writing formulas, and mechanical plot-generator games (such as Robo the Game That Writes a Million Story Plots) designed to automate or systematize narrative creation.'
  • T1-9 exhibitions and archives: 'Collaborative research projects, such as the Columbia University Literary AI Exhibition, explore how early writing techniques and manuals laid the groundwork for machine-generated prose and poetry.'
  • T1-10 era head: 'The Birth of Formal AI and Science Fiction (1950s–Present)'
  • T1-11 Dartmouth: 'John McCarthy and his colleagues formally coined the term "artificial intelligence," proposing that every aspect of learning or intelligence could be simulated by a machine—an idea that heavily mirrored literary and philosophical explorations of the possible.'
  • T1-12 utopian and dystopian visions: 'Science fiction literature repeatedly split AI into dual trajectories: helpful companions (like Star Trek's Data or Star Wars's R2-D2) versus existential threats.'
  • T1-13 symbolic logic to deep learning: 'Modern large language models trace their lineage back through decades of debate between rule-based symbolic AI and connectionist neural networks, arriving at contemporary transformer-based text generation.'
  • T1-14 closing offer: 'Would you like to explore a specific era (such as 19th-century gothic fiction or mid-century cybernetics) or focus on how modern LLMs relate to early plot generators?' (no marker)

Literary AI is an exhibit of Columbia's Rare Book & Manuscript Library, made by the Columbia English Department, the library and Columbia's Digital Scholarship department, on literature and computation as the Columbia Library's holdings show them. In eight cases with a credits page, copyright 2022 by Columbia University Libraries under CC-BY 4.0, built with Minicomp/Wax and linked to GitHub, it presents early debates over writing as skill or gift and as repeatable algorithm, and asks whether writing is a craft like any other. Its timeline runs circa 1890–1970 through manuals, devices and techniques that promised to ease or automate writing; it shows machine-written prose and poetry beside literature written with combinatorial devices, in two stories, production and analysis. Production: writing manuals, Hill's Plot Genies, Cook's Plotto, plot generators with spinning devices, the patents of Blanchard and Montague, Strachey's 1940s love letter program and Masterman's computer-aided translation. The mid-century question of frames or grammar, the exhibit says, drew on literary genre and linguistic rule and shaped early chat bots, baseball analytics, defense training and match-making, and early popular writing texts shape today's machine learning tools for aviation accident reports and defense logistics. Analysis: Fansler's Types of Prose Narratives, Polti's thirty-six situations (1895), compendia of folk tales, Keeler's web-word diagrams and Carolyn Well's distillation of the mystery novel. Organizing story elements in databases, scrapbooks and notecards forecast zettelkasten, Evernote and Google Docs, storage became central to analysis and composition, and the exhibit sets early prose generation beside natural language processing, Siri, Alexa and medical diagnostics. Columbia's Narrative Intelligence Lab lists the project under curatorial work with Alex Gil, Melina Moe and Dennis Yi Tenen; its site is MIT-licensed, 2026, after a founding letter of February 2025. Wikipedia has no article under the exhibit's title. The phrase also names a wider subject: writing about AI as old as stories, from Homer's golden handmaidens and Apollonius's Talos to Shelley, Lang and Clarke, in Stuart Roberts's Cambridge story on the AI Narratives programme of the CFI and the Royal Society, whose report is dated 11 December 2019. The programme calls itself the first large-scale study of AI in popular culture, holds that stories about AI shape the future and finds them turning on control; Sarah Dillon calls such narratives a dataset, holds that science fiction long explored today's questions and that fiction and science shape each other, and asks which novels will teach AI, proposing that diverse narratives could feed AI's data. Čapek coined 'robot' for R.U.R., the 1921 play that introduced 'artificial people'. Aissatou Barry's Science Survey article of August 2026 asks whether an AI can tell a story worth telling and what becomes of human storytelling if machines write; language models learn textual patterns, help writers brainstorm and have begun to be authors, though studies find their writing thin. It raises the ownership of machine-written stories under copyright made for human creators, traces the concern to Butler's Erewhon (1872), splits fictional AI into companions such as Data, R2-D2 and WALL-E and threats such as HAL 9000, credits AI with transforming literary criticism and calls it perhaps the next stage of writing. An IEEE Computer Society article, 'Literature and Artificial Intelligence', gives a literary perspective on AI's history from the McCarthy–Minsky–Rochester–Shannon proposal; video cards carry Tenen's Literary Theory for Robots and short histories of AI, one beginning with Ada Lovelace.

The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence, also called Literary AI, is an online exhibit of Columbia University's Rare Book & Manuscript Library on the long, shared history of literature and computation, told through the Columbia Library's holdings. It is a collaboration between the Columbia English Department, the Columbia University Rare Books & Manuscript Library and Columbia University's Digital Scholarship department, a description the CU Narrative Intelligence Lab repeats in its own entry for the project. Its about page, On Literary AI, stands at literaryai.library.columbia.edu; the exhibit is laid out in eight cases with a credits page, its site copyright 2022 by Columbia University Libraries with its contents offered under a CC-BY 4.0 International License, built with Minicomp/Wax and linking a GitHub repository and a contact page. No founding date is stated: the census records the 2022 copyright line and an online exhibit, and neither whether a physical exhibition ran at the Rare Book & Manuscript Library nor when; Wikipedia has no article under the exhibit's title. The exhibit presents texts from early debates over whether writing was a skill to be honed or a gift to be appreciated, and whether the skills of writing could be learned and even made into repeatable algorithms, and it asks whether writing is like any other craft that can be learned and taught. Following a timeline from circa 1890 to 1970, it explores professional manuals, devices and techniques that promised to make writing easier and even to automate it, and it shows examples of algorithmic composition, prose and poetry written by machines, beside literature written with the aid of algorithmic and combinatorial devices. As a curated library exhibition it tracks two stories, production and analysis; its unit is an exhibited item, a manual, device, patent, program or analysis, arranged in the eight cases, and the census records no geography beyond the holdings being Columbia's. The first story, "AI & Literary Production: Romance, Mystery, and Defense Aeronautics", follows literature as a professional and technical craft through writing manuals and guides for churning out mystery or romance plots, such as Wycliffe Hill's Plot Genies, and plot generators such as William Wallace Cook's Plotto series. Some how-to manuals carried simple plot generators, with spinning devices or automatic number generators to guide would-be novelists past writers' block, and in the exhibit's account automated text generation catalyzed a wave of early 20th-century patents, from Arthur Blanchard's "movie-writer" machine to Henrietta Rose Montague's "name selector". The story follows the manuals into mid-twentieth-century computer experiments in algorithmic and automated writing, from Christopher Strachey, who wrote a love letter program in the 1940s, to Margaret Masterman, a linguist who pioneered the use of computers to aid automatic translation. In the exhibit's account the mid-twentieth century faced an existential question, whether programs should be written from frames or from grammar, situational specifics or universal linguistic structures, a divide that drew its vocabulary from comparing literary genres to linguistic rules and that would influence early chat bots, baseball analytics, defense training programs and match-making algorithms. The exhibit holds that early 20th-century popular texts for aspiring screenplay writers, romance novelists and pulp fictioneers influence and shape contemporary, machine learning-based tools used in automating aviation accident reports and defense logistics. The second story, "AI & Literary Analysis: Character types, story pieces, chat bots, and medical care", tracks the use of algorithms to analyze literature, from Columbia alumna Harriot Fansler's dissection of Types of Prose Narratives, which she called a "textbook for the story writer", to Georges Polti's Les trente-six situations dramatiques (1895), with the thirty-six situations he theorized as structuring human experience. It includes analyses and compendia of folk tales, diagrams of plot structures, among them Harry Stephen Keeler's "web-word" designs, and Carolyn Well's distillation of the mystery novel. In its account the interest in narrative analysis and plot visualization catalyzed techniques for organizing story elements: databases, scrapbooks and notecards forecast zettelkasten, Evernote and Google Docs, and information storage came to be understood as central both to analysis and to composition. It holds that early twentieth-century techniques for generating prose were paralleled by advances in natural language processing, which today animate narratively "intelligent" bots such as Apple's Siri and Amazon's Alexa and influence automated medical diagnostics, the exhibit's own account of how early writing techniques relate to later language processing. The Columbia University Narrative Intelligence Lab files the project under curatorial work, as Literary AI, and names on its entry Alex Gil, Melina Moe and Dennis Yi Tenen; the lab's site carries an MIT License dated 2026 and quotes its founding letter of February 2025. The census record names the three Columbia departments and no person, and the Capture Registry finds the three names on a card whose page the census did not save. A video card pairs Tenen's name with the title Literary Theory for Robots: How Computers Learned to Write, a work distinct from the exhibit. The traininglayerliterature.org layer census asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it, and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception, and it admits a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds. It enters the exhibit as an exhibition in its area of field history, the history and indexes of electronic, generative and computational literature, standing to the census as historical lineage, with no relation stated to another of its rows, and gives as the question the exhibit answers what devices, manuals and programs for producing and analysing literature preceded machine-learning text generation, as Columbia's library holds them, circa 1890 to 1970. In the census's record the exhibit's place in the layer is not applicable: it holds library items of circa 1890 to 1970 and records no text entering a machine-learning model, while its about page draws a line from these materials to contemporary machine learning-based tools; it is no evidence that any text entered a model, and no corpus or dataset. The exhibit names the authors and inventors of its items, from Hill and Cook to Strachey, Masterman, Fansler and Polti; how it attributes the machine-written prose and poetry it shows is not recorded on the saved page, since the eight cases, the credits and the exhibit's dates are unread. What the exhibit makes, in the record's terms, is algorithmic composition, plots produced by plot generators with spinning devices or number generators, and analyses that sort narrative into types, recorded as production and analysis; the record leaves unanswered whether any particular text entered a machine-learning model, and anything after circa 1970 beyond the about page's claims of influence. The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature apart from AI-generated literature, where the machine is writer, literature about AI, where it is subject, and procedural or computational poetry, where it is method, and sorts the contemporary field into four practices told apart by the direction of address. In writing through AI the machine is method or procedure, asking "What does the algorithm reveal?"; in writing for AI it is reader, asking "What should the machines learn, retrieve, and repeat?"; AI-generated poetry has a machine writer and a human reader, training-layer literature a human writer and a machine reader. Four lineages of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries converge on training-layer literature, among them the procedural lineage, which, from the Oulipo through electronic literature to contemporary computational poetics, established that composition can be delegated to systems; there the machine "is method, not yet addressee", and the lineage normalized its presence inside the poem. The census reads the exhibit as a historical field resource for that procedural lineage, the delegation of composition to devices and systems, where the machine is method and, in Strachey's program, writer; its timeline closes about 1970, it records no text entering a model, and the machine reader of the survey's fourth column is outside what it holds, so that it is no record of writing addressed to a machine reader. The archive names procedural and constraint writing, with electronic literature, among the comparators of its own literary corpus. Its account of machine composition, the second wing of training-layer literature, asks what an encountered work makes it possible for a machine to write, and holds that whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from are different questions. The exhibit's title also names a wider subject, the story of artificial intelligence in literature and fiction, which runs further back: a University of Cambridge story by Stuart Roberts, "From Homer to HAL: 3000 years of AI narratives", holds that writing about artificial intelligence is almost as old as stories, from the women of gold Homer's Hephaestus forges as handmaidens in the Iliad and the bronze Talos of Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica (300 BCE) to the mechanisation imagined by Mary Shelley, Fritz Lang and Arthur C. Clarke. Karel Čapek coined the term "robot" for his play R.U.R. (1921), in which artificial servants rise up against their masters and which introduced the idea of "artificial people". The story announces the AI Narratives research programme of Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and the Royal Society, in its own words the first large-scale project of its kind on how AI is portrayed in popular culture, whose report it dates to 11 December 2019; its researchers hold that the stories told about AI will bear on all futures, and its team found that many such narratives pivot on control. Sarah Dillon, a project lead, holds that today's questions about AI were long explored in science fiction, that such narratives are an important dataset and that fiction has influenced science as much as science has influenced fiction; she asks which novels are being chosen to "teach" AI morality and proposes that more diverse narratives could feed back into the language and data of actual AI systems. An article in The Science Survey by Aissatou Barry (11 August 2026) asks whether an AI can truly create a story worth telling and what happens to the value of human storytelling if a machine can write: large language models learn patterns from enormous amounts of text, some writers use them as brainstorming partners, AI "has started becoming the author", and studies find its writing weak in emotional depth, consistency and originality. It asks who owns a story an AI system writes, where copyright largely recognizes human creators, finds that literature predicted these concerns, among its earliest examples Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872), divides the AI of science fiction into helpful companions such as Data, R2-D2 and WALL-E and threats such as HAL 9000, holds that AI analysis has transformed literary criticism, and proposes that AI may be the next stage in writing's evolution. Other cards on the same words carry an article titled "Literature and Artificial Intelligence" from the IEEE Computer Society, a "literary" perspective on the history of artificial intelligence that cites the project proposal of McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon, and three short video histories of artificial intelligence, one on its origins in Ada Lovelace. The Capture Registry records that, asked for the exhibit's title on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview read the title as the name of a field of study and wrote that field's history in three eras, from Homer's Iliad to contemporary transformer-based text generation, mentioning the exhibit in the second; its first card was Cambridge's story. The registry finds that the first and third eras have no counterpart on the exhibit's page, that the second era is headed with the exhibit's dates and opens on one of its items, Polti, and that the composition carries the page's prose and poetry written by machines and leaves out its two stories, production and analysis. It finds the composition's one plot device on no saved page and its machine composition beginning at the 1956 Dartmouth Workshop, with Strachey's program, the census's point where the machine is writer, absent and Columbia University the one maker named. It sets the page's own line forward, to machine learning-based tools and to the question of frames or grammar, against the composition's line back through rule-based symbolic AI and connectionist neural networks and its offer to relate modern language models to early plot generators, and it reads the whole as a topic answer in which the exhibit is one bullet and its holdings, its three departments and Strachey's program are not carried.

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): At 'The Literary History of Artificial Intelligence' (T1, ten cards: B1 Cambridge's story of the AI Narratives programme, B2 the CU Narrative Intelligence Lab's entry for the exhibit, B3 the exhibit's about page, B4 Tableau's history of AI, unread (403), B5 an IEEE Computer Society article, unread (script-rendered), B6, B7, B9, B10 videos read through their titles, B8 a Science Survey article; 356 words in the answer body, no markers, and a closing offer) the composition writes the history its title names, in three eras, and gives the exhibit one bullet. Composed from its cards: the first era at card 1's grain, Homer's golden handmaidens, Talos, Čapek's 'robot' with card 4's 1921 (B1 F35, F37–F40; B4 F50); the second era under the exhibit's dates and objects (B3 F6, F10, F12, at a coarser grain), with Polti (F19) and the exhibit as 'Collaborative research projects, such as the Columbia University Literary AI Exhibition' (F2 in part) and its 'machine-generated prose and poetry' (F7); the third era's companions, Data and R2-D2, from card 8 (F67, F68), and its threats at a coarser grain (F69). Substituted reading: the exhibit's timeline and its 'manuals, devices, and techniques' (F6) head a section of general history, their subject moved from the exhibition to the period, as the Capture Registry finds (CAP-1-04); Polti, whom the exhibit places in its second story, the use of algorithms to analyze literature (F19), stands among 'Combinatorial Plot Devices' as an author 'arguing that all plots could be mapped and recombined', a reading of his thirty-six situations on no card (CAP-1-05); the exhibit's own line forward, to machine learning-based tools for aviation accident reports and defense logistics (F17), is composed as groundwork 'for machine-generated prose and poetry' (CAP-1-11). Limit dropped: the exhibit's two stories, production and analysis (F8), and its frame, the history of literature and computation through the Columbia Library's holdings (F3), so that the exhibit's period bounds a general era; the three departments named as 'Columbia University' (F2; CAP-1-08); Talos without Europa (F38). Available, not composed (B_D): the exhibit's named items, Hill's Plot Genies and Cook's Plotto (F10), Blanchard's and Montague's patents (F11), Strachey's 1940s love letter program and Masterman's translation work (F13), the census's point where the machine is writer (CAP-1-07); the frames-or-grammar question and its influence (F14–F16); the second story's Fansler, Keeler and Wells (F18, F20) and its account of storage and natural language processing (F21–F24); the debates over writing as skill or gift (F4, F5); the eight cases, licence and build (F1, F25–F28); the curators on card 2, Alex Gil, Melina Moe and Dennis Yi Tenen (F29–F31, F34; CAP-1-09); from card 1, the AI Narratives programme, its report and its researchers' claims, among them Dillon's question which novels are chosen to 'teach' AI and her proposal that diverse narratives could feed AI's data (F36, F41–F49); from card 8, machine authorship, its ownership and copyright, Erewhon, AI's effect on criticism (F57–F66, F70, F71); the IEEE article as an object of its own (F51) and Tenen's book (F53). Force raised: Polti's categorization of thirty-six situations composed as an argument 'that all plots could be mapped and recombined' (F19). Composed without attribution: the whole body, no sentence tied to a card; at the coarse grain of common knowledge for the first and third eras, recorded; the exhibit's own timeline and objects (F6) composed as the period's, at the exhibit's resolution, without the exhibit as their source, a breach under the grain rule (§4.4 D_pres). Assigned to another, denied: none. Content replaced by use: the closing offer ('Would you like to explore a specific era ...'), recorded under N_ext. Outside the cards: Frankenstein (1818), Lovelace's composing engines, 'Robo the Game That Writes a Million Story Plots', the 1956 date of the Dartmouth Workshop, the symbolic-connectionist debate and transformers, the era heads (alignment.T1_outside_cards).

Read against its own cards, the composition takes the exhibit's title for its topic and writes the topic at the grain of card 1 and card 8, which concern that topic; of the two cards that concern the exhibit it keeps the period, one item, the phrase 'prose and poetry written by machines' and the institution, and sets them inside the topic's second era as general history. What the exhibit holds in its own terms, the two stories, its named devices and patents, Strachey's program, the curators on card 2, stays on the cards; one plot device and the composing engines of Lovelace enter from outside them.

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds, in one claim space with the field's: the layer census's question for the exhibit and its kind (TLL-06–TLL-12, TLL-38), the record's answers on the layer, in_layer 'not applicable', no text entering a model, no corpus or dataset, the authors and inventors named and the attribution of machine-written texts unrecorded, the cases unread (TLL-15–TLL-18, TLL-24–TLL-26, TLL-39, TLL-33, TLL-34, TLL-36), its other fields with their basis in B3 (TLL-01–TLL-05, TLL-13, TLL-14, TLL-19–TLL-23, TLL-29–TLL-32, TLL-37); the census's reading of the exhibit as a historical field resource for #186's procedural lineage, where the machine is method and, in Strachey's program, writer, with the machine reader of the fourth column outside what it holds (TLL-27, TLL-28, TLL-35); #186's definition of training-layer literature apart from machine-as-writer, machine-as-subject and machine-as-method literature, its four practices told apart by the direction of address and its procedural lineage (O186-01–O186-07); #1543's machine composition and its two questions, new writing and true provenance (O1543-01, O1543-02); #1680's comparators (O1680-01); and the Capture Registry's findings on the composition at the title (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-12). Every archive claim is 'not surfaced' (§6.2): no card of T is an archive source. The field claims are composed as received, the topic's claims as the claims of a neighbouring subject the title names; where an archive claim stands beside a field claim (TLL-16 and TLL-26, the attribution of machine-written texts unrecorded, beside B3 F7 and F13; TLL-27 beside F13, Strachey's program; TLL-15 beside F17, the exhibit's line to machine learning-based tools; CAP-1-09 beside B2 F31, the curators), both are composed under P_coh within the one ontology.
